passages.text: After Peter had said this, Simon answered, ‘Since I see you cleverly hinting that the things written against the creator in the books are not true, tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God.’ Having said this, Simon went out. Peter said to the crowds standing there, ‘Even if Simon can harm us in no other way concerning God, at least he prevents you from hearing the words that can purify the soul.’ At these words from Peter, much murmuring arose among the crowds, who said, ‘What necessity is there to let him come in here and speak his blasphemies against God?’ Peter heard and said, ‘May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon. For, as the Lord said, “There will be false apostles, false prophets, sects, and ambitions for rule.” These, as I conjecture, will take their beginning from Simon, who blasphemes God, and cooperate in saying the same things against God as Simon does.’ Having said this with tears, he beckoned the crowds with his hand. As they came forward, he laid his hands on them, prayed, and dismissed them, telling them to assemble earlier in the morning. Having said this, and groaning, he went inside and slept without even taking food.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὔ[ριον ἀπὸ] τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου λόγων δείξω τὸν δημιουργὸν μὴ ἀνώτατον λέγοντα εἶναι θεόν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text infers the teacher as the unexpressed object of show and subject of saying from the explicit reference to the teacher's words; the creator is the subject of the being infinitive. A materially different direct attachment makes λέγοντα agree with τὸν δημιουργόν: I will show from your teacher's words the creator saying that he is not the highest God. The reference to the teacher's words motivates the main inference but does not make it explicit or uncontested.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γένοιτο μέχρι Σίμωνος ἀρκετὸν γενέσθαι τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς πειρασμὸν ἀνθρώπων λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wish concerns the sufficiency and limit of the testing discourse in Simon. May it suffice as far as Simon is a more literal alternative; the English does not change the wish into a prediction that no later blasphemy will occur.

The first noun can mean factions or schools and the second loves of ruling or power-seeking. Sects and ambitions for rule preserve both social division and desire for control, without assigning later denominational names.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition supplies this conjunction in editorial brackets. Its sense is translated as that, without claiming independent recovery of an unbroken witness.

The selected edition supplies the beginning of in the books within brackets, including part of the noun. The English translates the supplied complete expression; it does not invent additional lost wording or a dotted gap.

The selected edition brackets the completion of tomorrow and the following from. These supplied words are translated as printed; the translation is not a new reconstruction of their underlying witness.

The supplied print accents this as ἐὰν. The English follows the permissive infinitive sense allow, supported by accusative αὐτόν and infinitive λέγειν, rather than treating it as a conditional conjunction. The usual infinitive accent ἐᾶν would be a proposed accentual normalization, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected accent is claimed.
